lessons.title: Expansion and factoring
lessons.objective: Distribute with signs, collect like terms, factor common factors and simple quadratics, and check by expansion.
recall: Factor an entire expression, not selected added terms. Start with the greatest common factor; then match a quadratic's leading, middle, and constant coefficients.
Expansion is the reverse check for factorization. A matching single input is evidence at that input only; it does not prove a polynomial identity.

lessons.title: Linear equations and formula rearrangement
lessons.objective: Isolate a specified variable, state any divisor restrictions, and verify a proposed solution by substitution.
recall: An equation asserts equality. Apply the same reversible operation to both sides and check whether a divisor could be zero.
After collecting terms, a nonzero coefficient gives one solution; a true constant statement gives all real solutions; a false statement gives none. Verify candidates in the original relationship.
mistakes: Delete a constant on one side

Classify the remaining true or false constant statement.

Ignoring the operation's domain
State the nonzero condition and inspect the zero case in the original equation.

lessons.title: Inequalities and absolute value
lessons.objective: Express the full solution set of a linear, compound, or absolute-value inequality with correct endpoints.
recall: An inequality's answer is a set, not one convenient value. Dividing by a negative reverses order; adding the same number does not.

AND means overlap and OR means union. Absolute value measures distance, so compare the threshold with zero before drawing an inside interval or two outside regions. Infinity is never an included endpoint.
mistakes: Forget to reverse order
Treating a negative divisor like a positive one
Test one value on each side of the boundary in the original inequality.
Confuse AND with OR
Combining conditions without set meaning
Keep only shared values for AND; keep any permitted value for OR.
Include a strict endpoint
Ignoring equality condition
Substitute the endpoint and read the original relation.

lessons.title: Quadratics and complete root sets
lessons.objective: Choose a quadratic solution method, return every root in the requested number system, and verify the roots.
recall: Set the equation equal to zero before using the zero-product property. A ready-made square may make the square-root method shorter than factoring.

The discriminant predicts the real-root count. Keep both branches when solving a nonzero square and distinguish a repeated root from two distinct values. Use i squared equals -1 only when complex roots are requested.
mistakes: Drop the negative square-root branch

Substitute both signed candidates.
Use zero-product reasoning before making zero
Ignoring the property's hypothesis
Move all terms to one side first.
Report graph intercepts for nonreal roots
Number-system mismatch
A real graph has no real zero when the discriminant is negative.

lessons.title: Rational expressions and original restrictions
lessons.objective: Find common denominators, cancel factors only, state original exclusions, and divide rational expressions without dividing by zero.
recall: Record every original denominator zero before simplifying. Canceled factors still leave excluded inputs.

For division, the divisor must be defined and nonzero. For addition, use a common denominator and multiply the entire numerator by each missing factor. Retain any physical-domain restrictions separately.

lessons.title: Restrictions and extraneous solutions
lessons.objective: Solve rational and radical equations while preserving original restrictions and rejecting invalid candidate roots.
recall: Record the original domain first. Multiplying by an excluded denominator or squaring a relation may admit candidates that were not original solutions.
After transforming, check every candidate in the original equation. Distinguish an undefined expression from a defined but false equality; both reject the candidate for different reasons.
